description: With Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie opened the chapter of radioactivity. Two Nobel Prizes, a crushing workload, and an immense legacy.

hero.hook: She processed tons of ore to isolate a few grams of an invisible element.

blocks.text: **Marie Curie**, born Maria Skłodowska, was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize. She is still the only person to have won **two** of them in two different sciences: physics, then chemistry.
Her subject was **radioactivity**, the fact that certain atoms spontaneously give off energy and particles.
Born in Poland, she left to study in Paris because the universities at home closed many doors to women. She worked hard, often in makeshift conditions.
She married the physicist **Pierre Curie**. Together they formed a laboratory partnership that was rare for the time.
In **1896**, **Henri Becquerel** noticed that uranium fogged photographic plates with no light involved. Marie Curie decided to study the phenomenon in detail. She coined the word **radioactivity**.

blocks.caption: Tons of pitchblende to isolate radium and polonium

blocks.text: With Pierre she discovered two new elements: **polonium**, named after Poland, and **radium**. Isolating them meant processing huge quantities of an ore called pitchblende.
Radium glows faintly in the dark. People marveled at it first, and only later understood how dangerous it was.

In **1903**, Marie, Pierre and Becquerel received the Nobel Prize in Physics. In **1911**, Marie received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry on her own. Pierre died in an accident in 1906. She kept working.
During the First World War she organized mobile X-ray units to help treat the wounded. She exposed her own body to doses that we would judge unacceptable today.

sections.title: Glory and the price to pay

blocks.text: Radioactivity made radiation therapy against some cancers possible, and it made nuclear weapons possible too. Knowledge itself is neutral. What people do with it is not.
Marie Curie turned a strange observation into a new science: radioactivity. Her work opened the way to modern physics, at the cost of risks nobody understood at the time.
